Soil Suitability analysis
Reading in the data

info_ACRPC = pd.read_parquet(soil_path/"info_ACRPC_Soil_Septic.parquet")
info_BCRC = pd.read_parquet(soil_path/"info_BCRC_Soil_Septic.parquet")
info_CCRPC = pd.read_parquet(soil_path/"info_CCRPC_Soil_Septic.parquet")
info_CVRPC = pd.read_parquet(soil_path/"info_CVRPC_Soil_Septic.parquet")
info_LCPC = pd.read_parquet(soil_path/"info_LCPC_Soil_Septic.parquet")
info_MARC = pd.read_parquet(soil_path/"info_MARC_Soil_Septic.parquet")
info_NWRPC = pd.read_parquet(soil_path/"info_NWRPC_Soil_Septic.parquet")

geom_ACRPC = gpd.read_parquet(soil_path/"geom_ACRPC_Soil_Septic.parquet")
geom_BCRC = gpd.read_parquet(soil_path/"geom_BCRC_Soil_Septic.parquet")
geom_CCRPC = gpd.read_parquet(soil_path/"geom_CCRPC_Soil_Septic.parquet")
geom_CVRPC = gpd.read_parquet(soil_path/"geom_CVRPC_Soil_Septic.parquet")
geom_LCPC = gpd.read_parquet(soil_path/"geom_LCPC_Soil_Septic.parquet")
geom_MARC = gpd.read_parquet(soil_path/"geom_MARC_Soil_Septic.parquet")
geom_NWRPC = gpd.read_parquet(soil_path/"geom_NWRPC_Soil_Septic.parquet")

making a plot to see the geometry data

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 10))

geom_ACRPC.plot(ax=ax, color='lightgray')
geom_BCRC.plot(ax=ax, color='blue')
geom_CCRPC.plot(ax=ax, color='purple')
geom_CVRPC.plot(ax=ax, color='green')
geom_LCPC.plot(ax=ax, color='orange')
geom_MARC.plot(ax=ax, color='yellow')
geom_NWRPC.plot(ax=ax, color='red')

plt.show()








What this plot shows is that we do not have all of the soil suitability data. We are missing some of Northeastern Vermont, Central Vermont, and a bit of Southeastern Vermont as well. While there is still a lot of data available, this merits future research to see if there is soil suitability data available for the regional planning commissions that we don’t have data for.
getting the amount of each soil suitability level for each regional planning commission

import numpy as np


info_soil_data = [info_ACRPC, info_CCRPC, info_CVRPC, info_LCPC, info_MARC, info_NWRPC, info_BCRC]
whole_vermont_info = pd.concat(info_soil_data, ignore_index=True)
info_soil_data.append(whole_vermont_info)
info_soil_data_name = ["ACRPC", "CCRPC", "CVRPC", "LCPC", "MARC", "NWRPC", "BCRC", "Vermont"]

for i in range(len(info_soil_data)):
    # print(info_soil_data[i].sort_values(by='Suitability').groupby(['Suitability'])['Acres'].sum())
    # print(np.sort(info_soil_data[i]['Suitability'].unique()))
    plt.bar(height = info_soil_data[i].sort_values(by='Suitability').groupby(['Suitability'])['Acres'].sum(), x = np.sort(info_soil_data[i]['Suitability'].unique()))
    plt.xticks(rotation = 45)
    plt.title(f"Soil Suitability Distribution by Acres for {info_soil_data_name[i]}")
    plt.xlabel("Soil Suitability Level")
    plt.ylabel("Number of Acres")
    plt.show()

whole_vermont_info = pd.concat(info_soil_data, ignore_index=True)

























































What these charts are going over is the number of acres of each level of soil suitability for septic tanks for each regional planning commission, as well as Vermont as a whole. There is an important caveat that the Vermont section is not all of Vermont, but rather all of the data we have, as there are a few regional planning commissions who’s data we don’t have.
What these charts show is that there is a lot of variability between regions in terms of the distribution of soil suitability. By this I mean that some regional planning commissions have radically different soil suitabilities, with one example being that the NWRCP has ‘not suited’ as by far its largest soil suitability level, while for BCRC ‘moderately suited’ is its largest soil suitability level, with ‘not suited’ coming in a distant second.
Looking a Vermont as a whole, either ‘not suited’ or ‘moderately suited’ is the largest soil suitability level for most regions, though CVRCP bucks that trend with ‘marginally suited’ being its most common soil suitability level. This frequency is shown on the Vermont total numbers, with ‘not suited’ being the most common soil suitability level, ‘moderately suited’ being the next most common, and ‘marginally suited’ being a close third. While the top 3 are all pretty close in terms of acres, the other two, ‘not rated’ and ‘well suited’, have a lot fewer acres. What this means for Vermont as a whole is a lot of its land is not really suited for septic tanks between all the acres that are ‘not suited’ or ‘marginally suited’. After that a good amount of land is ‘moderately suitable’, indicating that septic tanks could be placed there, though conditions are not perfect for it. And lastly, there is a relatively small percentage of land that is ‘well suited’, and no regions have ‘well suited’ as their top two most common soil suitability levels, indicating that no region of Vermont is perfect for septic systems.

Northeast Vermont, as identified by earlier graphs, is one of the locations in Vermont with the lowest density of wastewater treatment service areas to its total land, and so the lack of information about suitability for septic tanks, which are an alternative to a public sewage systems which is represented by the wastewater treatment service areas.

Adding in more features
Next block is using pandas to describe the data.
The region of each state is determined by the census, coming from this website: https://www2.census.gov/geo/pdfs/maps-data/maps/reference/us_regdiv.pdf
The regions and their acronym’s - New England: NE - Middle Atlantic: MA - East North Central: ENC - West North Central: WNC - South Atlantic: SA - East South Central: ESC - West South Central: WSC - Mountain: M - Pacific: P - Whole United States: US This block will make a list of the column names. It will also print out all the unique state abbreviations, which will total 52, one for each state, the district of columbia, and the United States of America as a whole. It will also add each state to its census region, with the acroynm’s listed above. Finally, a new database will be created with fewer columns, keeping the ones more relevant to the analysis that will be conducted. This means keeping the overall numbers for different professions, but not specifics like the number of new graduates or the number of male or female practitioners.

title: Vermont Data Collaborative Data Engineering
text:
Getting Started

Reading through vision and codebase_primer markdowns

backend is for data, website hosting, and run time logic

data folder has lots of different raw data files, and the processed data files which are parquet files to be easily used with sql
API brings info from data to frontend
Query does a similar thing, but with the more complex runtime logic
Build cleans the data, turns in into the parquet files, and then makes a permenant sql file
Data_collection is how the data is collected, using web scrapers
notebooks are the walkthrough for easier understanding of the backend
app_utils: everything that needs to get cleaned up and reorganized

frontend is for the website

most of it is handled by node.js and npm
src is the typescript that makes the website

app is the pages for the website
components holds the “functions” that are needed for multiple pages
lib are other projects that work in concert with the data stuff
markdown: place to store markdowns. not really sure why it exists though
utils, it is a way of turning some items into other items, which is useful for parts of the javascript



cascading filter

the idea of a cascading filter makes sense to me
it works by narrowing done the field of focus progressively so that its easy and simple to do
for zoning, this works by first narrowing the county level, then the jurisdiction, then the district name, then finally the district type
at any point, someone can stop filtering, but the cascading filter makes it easy to keep going




Getting Familiar

backend zoning tooltip

GDF stands for geodataframe
the function process_zoning_data first calls a function to clean the data

it then calls a function that adds fill colors through a color map that is added to the geodataframe in a new column
it then finally calls a function to create the tooltip

the function to create a tooltip, called add_zoning_tooltip which then calls add_tooltip_from_dict

this then creates a new column in the geodataframe for the tooltip
this new column holds the plain text used to create a python dictionary, with each label in that dictionary holding the value of the corresponding column

that is defined by the label_to_col dictionary passed in to the function


the zoning specific parts of this are the unique data cleaning, and the unique label_to_col dictionary, everything else is generalizable
how the tooltip is shown to the user (my guess)

I looked at the front end code, and got really confused and could not figure it out
so my guess is the tooltip is turned into a dictionary that allows for unique labels when hovering over different zoning districts
this is because the tooltip does not include the geospatial coordinates, just facts about the zoning districts that would be useful to know when hovered over.


data engineering

goals are to have clean and orderly code
separation between collecting, cleaning, run-time query stuff, serving the data to the frontend
make it easy to cross-reference datasets and filter them
have the ability for llms to get involved in the future
uses a filtering scheme in a schema.json file

this works with a primary dataset and a secondary dataset that is being joined to the primary one
there is a join key (what column is being joined on)
there is a join type (what kind of join)
and there is a list of ordered label-column pairs that create the cascading filter

tidy data article

tidy datasets provide a standardized way of linking the structure and meaning of a dataset
in tidy data:

each variable forms a column
each observation forms a row
each kind of observable unit makes a table

variables are generally easier to define functional relationships between, and easier to make comparisons between groups of observations
for myself: tidy data often needs melting of the original dataset

the schema.json file

it defines the joining and filtering for the filter tree on the primary dataset. for this file, the only primary dataset option currently is the default one

for the filter tree, it then takes the ‘source’, whether the dataset it zoning_info or zoning_rules, and takes the info for columns stored in the json and returns it

basically, the json file holds the join information for different datasets, as well as the columns for their cascading filters

how the filters work

the information about them is stored in the json file, specifically in the columns section. the columns section is an ordered list of the cascading filters
the difference between the primary dataset and secondary dataset keys does not really exist. the primary dataset key gets matched to the secondary dataset key to combine the two datasets
for filtering the zoning and census query question

the primary dataset would be the zoning dataset
the secondary dataset would be the census dataset
the join key would be the spatial coordinates
the join type would be a spatial join
i imagine the columns would be: county and town name for the census dataset



table_build qmd

basically just does all of the data cleaning and checking in a qmd notebook before moving the code to a build script
it is a way of more cleanly showing how the tables the website uses are built

build script for zoning

it creates functions to do basically every different step in the previous qmd notebook
basically, it does the same thing as the qmd notebook, just in a way that can get run as part of the greater website
the final names of the tables it produces are info, colors, geom, and rules

these table names come from what they represent. info for the information about the zoning district, colors for the color mapping, geom for the geometric coordinates, and rules for the specific zoning rules of each zoning district


core functions script

build_where_query_from_filters: my assumption is it takes the filters from the cascading filters and turns it into a sql query
FilterSource is a basic class for cascading filter requests (connects backend to frontend)
compile_cte: creates a sql string that selects each unique value of the join key, where each column being filtered in is in the filtered amount

basically if we are filtering by addison county (municipal district), then select each distinct key where its column of municipal district is in the list of [‘addison county’]
*this took me a long time to figure out

compile_join: creates a sql string that does the right join
compile_filters: creates two strings, each compiled into larger sql strings

one being all the compile_cte for the filters coming in (i think only ever 2)
the other one being the compile_join for each filter coming in

sql_filter_block

recreates the where block needed to do the compile_cte
then reads a SQL file, using the format function to dictate specific sql code blocks get added where to the SQL file being read

note: not to the literal file, but to the text copy of it being read at the moment

and the updated text of the SQL file with compile_cte and join_cte slotted in to the right places specified for them in the original SQL file


zoning.py in query section

the file reads in sql commands through the sql_filter_block function from the core_functions script
the sql is also stored in the sql folder in the queries folder
to reduce the code, the functions for geodata and zoning rules could probably be combined, with the new function having an input for whether or not it is geo data

zoning code in the API section

The frontend finds what filters the SQL needs through the POST request. Specifically, where on the website the POST request is coming through decides the function used, and the post request delievers a list of categories to filter by (I believe)
I would imagine there is not anything in the schema about the fourth table build, the colors table, because it is already joined to every table in its each sql statement, so there is no need for a schema
how to zoning code actually works is that it runs the sql_filter_block function with the filters given to it by the POST request

It then runs a function to execute that filter block, and returns the data selected to the API


Reflection Time :)

General Philosophy: Task has its own section, and each section does its own task

this is to say that each part of the pipeline, from data collection to creating the website, happens in discrete steps in different files

Things that could be improved

Give me some more time to think on this

it took a long time to read through and start to understand how the code is organized, but it is quite organized and systematic which is good






Problems/ I have noticed in the setup

some of the react dependencies are out of date, and it said there were critical flaws

did not take a screenshot

conda environment just could not recognize a lot of packages (i had to install uvicorn and fastapi in pip)

some of that could be my computer, some of that could

there was no frontend.env.local file on github
node.js/nvm setup was hard. got it downloaded on my root of the terminal, and then it would not work in each directory until i specified it

seems just the way this is
trick is to download it in the root, then navigate to the specific directory and try to download again
it automatically updated which directories node.js and nvm would work in, which was nice without downloading node.js a second time

read.me steps goes from 1 to 3 with no step 2

title: Report
text:
Plotting
The goal of this section is to now dive into how Vermont compares to the United States, as well as other states like Vermont
The code chunk below does the plotting for the first plot
What this plot is supposed to show is the ratio of different workers in different health care professions in Vermont compared to the US as a whole. This will be helpful in understanding how Vermont’s healthcare system compares to the US.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

plt.figure(figsize=(12, 5))
plt.xticks(rotation=90)
sns.barplot(data=small_combined_ratio_melted, x='occupation', y='ratio', hue='st_abbrev')
plt.title("Bar Plot Comparing the Ratio of Different Kinds of Health Care Professionals to the\nTotal Population for Vermont and the United States")
plt.show()








Looking at the plot now, we see that Vermont has more physicians than the US on average, and tends to have a slightly higher ratio of health professionals in general. While there are a number of professions where there is no blue bar, this is because there was no data collected for those professions, rather than there being basically no one practicing them. Besides the fact that the professions with no data in Vermont are generally the least numerous professions, I know that at least some of the lack of data is because it is not collected not that there is no one practicing those professions, as one bar with no data is ot_23, standing for occupational therapist and I know there are occupational therapists currently practicing in Vermont.
The code chunk below does the plotting for the second plot

plt.figure(figsize=(12, 5))
plt.xticks(rotation=90)
sns.barplot(data=vt_and_ne_ratio_melted, x='occupation', y='ratio', hue='st_abbrev')
plt.title("Bar Plot Comparing the Ratio of Different Kinds of Health Care Professionals to the\nTotal Population for Vermont and the Rest of the Northeast")
plt.show()








This plot takes looking at the whole of the United States, and narrows it down to the rest of the northeast. This means that Vermont is being compared to similar states, namely Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, and Rhode Island. This was done by adding the the profession numbers as well as the populations of those states together, and dividing the profession numbers by the summed population to get a ratio of professionals to population for the entire Northeast leaving out Vermont. Vermont is left out because there are not too a lot of states in the Northeast, and if Vermont was left in, its numbers would skew the Northeast average closer to Vermont’s, and the goal here is not to find the northeast average, but to compare Vermont’s health care profession ratio’s to other similar states.
Looking at the results, we can see that Vermont and the other Northeast States are pretty similar. For most of the ratio’s, we can see that the other Northeast States have on average slightly more health-care professionals compared to their total population. That being said, Vermont does have a substantially larger ratio of counselors and personal care aides, as well as slightly more social workers, repository therapists, speech pathologists, and massage therapists.

title: Report
text:
Conclusion
In conclusion, Vermont is similar to the rest of the Northeast when it comes to the ratio of health care professionals to its total population. That being said, the Northeast as a whole has a larger ratio of health professionals to its population, and Vermont tends to have ratios greater than the United States as a whole.
If your looking for something surprising, the amount of counselors Vermont has is quite surprising, with its ratio being about double the ratio that the United States had. Beyond that, there was nothing too surprising in the data to me as a non-expert, though if you are an expert some of the numbers might be more shocking.
While I am wrapping up this project right now, if I have more time to devote to this then doing analysis on the cosine similarly of and k-means clustering on the ratio’s of health professions between states would be interesting. I picked the Northeast region as a whole when looking for other states that are similar to Vermont, but it would be interesting seeing what the data actually says about which states are similar.
